---
title: "Triangular Numbers: Count All Contiguous Subarrays"
description: "An interview maths technique with symbols, numbers and an independent proof."
---

## When this technique appears

When a nested-loop problem counts all intervals or pairs of indices.

## The question

**Why are there exactly n(n+1)/2 nonempty contiguous subarrays?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\ell=\frac{n(n+1)}2
$$

**Every symbol explained:** n is array length; ℓ ranges from 1 through n and denotes a subarray length; Σ adds the number of subarrays over lengths, while the right side is the triangular-number identity.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For n=4, there are 4 subarrays of length 1, 3 of length 2, 2 of length 3 and 1 of length 4, totalling 4+3+2+1=10=4×5/2.

## Prove the mathematical step

A subarray of length ℓ can start in n−ℓ+1 positions. Summing over lengths from 1 to n is 1+2+...+n. Pair first and last terms to derive n(n+1)/2.

## Common mistake or limitation

Subarrays are contiguous and include repeated values at different positions as different intervals. The count differs from the 2^n subsets of an array.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Every start i admits n−i ending positions; adding the decreasing counts yields the triangular number.**

Practise by speaking the argument, not reciting the formula alone.

**Interview problems:** Count Subarrays; All Pairs of Indices.

**Research reference:** [See the underlying method](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/binomial-coefficients.html). The worked examples and explanation are original.
